strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for speech language models: preserving reconstruction quality while reducing the number of acoustic codebook channels. The proposed masking mechanism targets a concrete limitation of conventional residual quantization.

Reconstruction evaluation covers LibriTTS test-clean, test-other, and LJSpeech using complementary metrics. Four-channel results show useful improvements: on test-clean, PESQ increases from 2.4026 with Vocos to 2.6329, and speaker similarity increases from 0.7892 to 0.8463.

Downstream evaluation includes both VALL-E and MobileSpeech, with human ratings on 50 samples and at least 10 listeners per audio. Speaker similarity improves over EnCodec+Vocos for both models, providing evidence of practical utility beyond reconstruction.
The manuscript reports several training settings and provides a link for code and pretrained models, offering a useful foundation for reuse.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not isolated experimentally. Section 4.5 compares pretrained EnCodec/Vocos components against Language-Codec trained on a different, substantially larger dataset. Consequently, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to MCRVQ. A controlled RVQ-versus-MCRVQ comparison using the same data, encoder, decoder, and training budget is needed to substantiate the proposed mechanism.

The claimed reduction in the text-to-acoustic modeling gap remains indirect. There is no quantitative analysis of information distribution or text-conditioned prediction difficulty across channels, and no measurement of downstream computational savings. Table 2 does not specify the codebook counts used. WER and prosody change little, while MOS improvements over EnCodec+Vocos are modest relative to the reported uncertainty; paired statistical analysis would help establish their reliability.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Section 3.3 and Equation 5 do not clearly specify the channel-specific temporal masks, their inference behavior, or the cumulative residual and fusion operations. Figure 1 labels components 'RVQ (transformer)' without explaining those transformers. Codebook sizes, loss weights, and exact decoder settings are also missing. The 20,000 hours of internal data and unspecified corpus sampling further limit independent training reproduction.

Reported results require reconciliation. Table 3 gives LJSpeech UTMOS scores of 3.7091/3.8955 for four/eight channels, whereas Table 4 reports 3.8549/4.0127 for apparently identical configurations. Claims of superiority across all objective metrics also exceed the evidence: SpeechTokenizer achieves higher UTMOS at both channel counts on test-clean and LJSpeech. These discrepancies and metric tradeoffs should be addressed before the results support a clear Findings recommendation.

The comparison set omits directly relevant approaches discussed or cited in the paper, particularly HiFi-Codec and improved RVQGAN. SpeechTokenizer is absent from downstream comparisons despite targeting the same representation-alignment problem. Furthermore, evaluation on English read speech provides limited support for the broader multilingual and real-world generalization motivation.
